title: Divide and Conquer and Merge Sort

questions.prompt: What is merge sort's worst-case time complexity?
questions.explanation: Merge sort is Θ(n log n) in every case — the recursion tree has log n levels, each doing Θ(n) merge work.

questions.prompt: Is the standard array-based merge sort in-place?

options.text: No — it needs O(n) auxiliary space for merging
Yes — it sorts using O(1) extra space
Yes — it swaps elements like quicksort
Only when the input is already sorted

questions.explanation: The merge step writes into an auxiliary array, so merge sort uses O(n) extra space and is not in-place.

questions.prompt: Which statements about merge sort are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is stable when ties are taken from the left half
Its Θ(n log n) bound holds for every input
The merge step runs in linear time
It sorts in place with O(1) extra space

questions.explanation: Merge sort is stable, guaranteed Θ(n log n), and its merge is linear. It is NOT in-place — it uses O(n) auxiliary space.

questions.prompt: Merge sort's recurrence is T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + ______, where the added term is the linear-time merge. (write the growth term, e.g. O(n))
questions.explanation: The merge of two halves is linear, so the combine cost is Θ(n); the recurrence solves to Θ(n log n).

questions.prompt: Order the three steps of the divide-and-conquer paradigm as applied by merge sort.

items.text: Divide the array into two halves
Combine: merge the two sorted halves

questions.explanation: Divide and conquer splits the problem, solves the pieces recursively, then combines — here the combine step is the linear merge.

questions.prompt: Match each merge-sort property with its value.
questions.explanation: Merge sort trades O(n) extra space for a guaranteed Θ(n log n), stable, but non-in-place sort.
